library(jsonlite)

read_json_file <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json_file("pre_colonial_sultanates_and_philippines.json5")

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

fmt_coord <- function (arg0_coords) {
  if (is.null(arg0_coords) || length(arg0_coords) < 2) return("NA")
  lat <- as.numeric(arg0_coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(arg0_coords[[2]])
  lat_s <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S")
  lon_s <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  paste0(lat_s, ", ", lon_s)
}

reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
all_years <- names(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark)
tot_1200 <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1200"]])
tot_1786 <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1786"]])
tot_area <- as.numeric(mod_data$total_area_km2)

# Abstract

The maritime realm of island Southeast Asia and the Philippine archipelago (2,07M km², comprising 2.073.299 km² and 26.777 active 5-arcminute terrestrial grid cells) accommodated one of the most dynamic nautical trade ecologies of the mediaeval and early modern globe. Extending from the Strait of Malacca and the volcanic alluvial plains of central and eastern Java to the clove-bearing volcanic cones of Maluku, the estuarine river mouths of coastal Borneo, the Bugis-Makassar thalassocracies of southern Sulawesi and the coastal barangays of pre-Spanish Luzon and the Visayas, this maritime space evolved through the convergence of rice agriculture, forest collecting and long-distance oceanic commerce. The period between 1200AD and 1786AD witnessed the progressive Islamisation of major trading ports, the rise and dissolution of regional sultanates and the initial transformations wrought by Iberian and Dutch mercantile intrusions.

Reconstructed across eight insular and peninsular sub-regions under MANDALA, regional population expanded from 7,50M inhabitants in 1200AD (yielding an aggregate density of 361,74 persons per 100 km²) to 9,40M in 1400AD, 10,80M in 1500AD and 11,60M in 1565AD at the arrival of the Legazpi expedition. Sustained demographic growth continued throughout the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries despite epidemic shocks and monopolistic trade blockades, reaching 12,20M in 1600AD, 13,80M in 1700AD and 15,80M by 1786AD (attaining an aggregate regional density of 762,07 persons per 100 km²). Throughout this trajectory, Java functioned as the demographic anchor of the archipelago, expanding from 3,15M in 1200AD to 6,64M in 1786AD, supported by intensive sawah wet-rice cultivation along the Brantas and Solo river basins.

Demographic mass followed distinct ecological specialisations across the macro-region. In 1786AD, Java accommodated 42,0% of total population (6,64M inhabitants; 4.947,92 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the inland agrarian capital of Mataram (Kotagede and Plered) and commercial ports such as Jayakarta, Banten Lama and Surabaya. Sumatra supported 2,53M people (16,0%; 524,12 persons per 100 km²), concentrated in the pepper-growing domains of Aceh, the Minangkabau highlands and the riverine basin of Palembang. Pre-Spanish and early colonial Luzon and the Visayas supported 1,74M inhabitants (11,0%; 873,66 persons per 100 km²), anchored by the Manila Bay polities of Tondo and Maynila alongside lacustrine settlements around Laguna de Bay. Southern Sulawesi housed 1,42M people (9,0%; 750,45 persons per 100 km²), propelled by the twin maritime kingdoms of Gowa-Tallo and Bone. The Malay Peninsula supported 1,11M residents (7,0%; 807,77 persons per 100 km²), centred historically on the international entrepôt of Melaka and successor river capitals in Johor and Perak. Coastal Borneo supported 948k people (6,0%; 126,95 persons per 100 km²), while the Sulu and Maguindanao sultanates housed 790k (5,0%; 774,81 persons per 100 km²) and the Maluku spice islands supported 632k (4,0%; 763,38 persons per 100 km²).

This historical demographic synthesis integrates 2.422 catalogued settlement trajectories with systematic multi-temporal archaeological surveys, ceramic sherding densities, radiocarbon sequences and indigenous archival chronicles. By isolating nucleated urban and coastal entrepôt populations from dasymetrically allocated rural swidden and sawah cultivators, the reconstruction captures the functional division between coastal mercantile thalassocracies and interior agrarian hinterlands. The results demonstrate that while external naval intervention altered trade routes and disrupted urban port hierarchies, rural demographic expansion remained resilient across the fertile volcanic soils and river valleys of the archipelago.

# Background

## Maritime Geography and Monsoon Circulation

The insular geography of the Malay Archipelago and the Philippine islands represents an extraordinary maritime crossroads structured by shallow epicontinental seas, narrow straits and alternating monsoon wind regimes [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Jones2018Some]. The Sunda Shelf connects Sumatra, Java, Borneo and the Malay Peninsula across shallow waters, creating navigable sea lanes sheltered from open ocean swells. To the east, Wallacea and the deep oceanic basins of Sulawesi, Maluku and the Philippine archipelago present a fragmented geography of volcanic archipelagos, coral atolls and rugged mountainous islands whose human populations developed deep insular adaptations across millennia of maritime migration [@M2021Multiple].

Monsoon winds governed regional connectivity and demographic mobility throughout the pre-colonial era [@Widodo2018Morphology]. The southwest monsoon carried maritime merchants from the Indian Ocean, the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea eastward through the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait from June to September. Conversely, the northeast monsoon powered shipping southward from mainland China, Taiwan and Japan into the Philippine inland seas, the Sulu Sea and the Java Sea from December to March. This rhythmic climatic pulse fostered coastal entrepôts whose demographic profiles swelled during trading seasons with transient populations of foreign merchants, artisans and seafaring crews [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Jones2018Some].

Ecologically, the macro-region encompasses two contrasting agrarian regimes:
1. Intensive volcanic sawah rice agriculture: Concentrated in central and eastern Java, western Sumatra (the Minangkabau highland plateaus) and the river plains of southwestern Sulawesi. Volcanic ash deposits continuously replenished soil fertility, enabling multi-cropping, high rural population densities and the extraction of agricultural surpluses capable of supporting inland royal courts and military levies [@Wood2008Volcano; @Faral2022Year].
2. Swidden cultivation and coastal foraging: Characteristic of the heavily forested interiors of Borneo, Sumatra, Mindanao and Luzon, where communities practised long-fallow shifting cultivation of dry rice, root crops and sago palm exploitation, combined with intensive marine and mangrove foraging [@M2021Multiple; @MJB2025Insights].

## The Islamisation of Island Southeast Asia

During the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the ideological and commercial organisation of maritime Southeast Asia underwent profound restructuring through the progressive adoption of Islam by coastal rulers [@DeJosselinDe1960Malacca; @Borschberg2016Melaka]. Earlier Hindu-Buddhist courtly paradigms, manifested in the monumental stone architecture of Central Java and the maritime hegemony of Srivijaya, gave way to coastal Islamic sultanates that drew ideological legitimacy from pan-Islamic trade networks, legal institutions and sacral concepts of royal sovereignty [@Zaharani2025Concept; @Arifia2024Batee].

The adoption of Islam proceeded along major trade arteries:
- Northern Sumatra and Western Java: Samudera Pasai emerged as an early Islamic sultanate in the late thirteenth century, followed by the rapid ascendancy of the Sultanate of Aceh at the northern tip of Sumatra. Aceh established close diplomatic, commercial and epigraphic links with the Sultanate of Banten in western Java, evidenced by shared mortuary traditions and coastal defensive alliances against European fleets [@Arifia2024Batee; @Kemper2019Umbilical].
- The Strait of Malacca: Founded around 1400AD, the Sultanate of Melaka embraced Islam and transformed into the foremost global trade emporium of the fifteenth century, establishing a codified legal framework (Undang-Undang Melaka) and maritime customs code that defined Malay statecraft across the peninsula [@DeJosselinDe1960Malacca; @Borschberg2016Melaka; @Tachimoto1998Malacca].
- Coastal Java (Pesisir): Northern coastal towns such as Demak, Jepara, Tuban and Gresik converted to Islam through merchant guilds and Sufi teachers. Demak led the military confederation that displaced the declining Majapahit empire in the early sixteenth century, fostering trading contacts that extended from the Sunda Strait to eastern Indonesia [@Kemper2019Umbilical; @Knaap2006About].
- Borneo and the Eastern Archipelagos: The Sultanate of Brunei expanded its tributary sphere across coastal Borneo and the southwestern Philippines, consolidating royal authority through hereditary aristocratic structures [@Morris1974Brunei; @Harrison1973Brunei]. In Maluku, the rival spice sultanates of Ternate and Tidore adopted Islam in the late fifteenth century, projecting naval power across Halmahera, Seram and the Papuan coast [@Rusdiyanto2018Kesultanan; @Charney1996World; @Clercq1890Staatsievl].
- Southern Philippines: The Sultanates of Sulu and Maguindanao coalesced as formidable Islamic thalassocracies in Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago, combining diplomatic statecraft with expansive maritime trade and naval defence [@Clav2025Beyond; @Mendoza2015Landlessness].

## Entrepôt Urbanism and Port Polities

Urbanism in pre-colonial maritime Southeast Asia was characterised by distinctive architectural and spatial typologies that differed fundamentally from stone-walled continental cities [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Mustaffa2023Tracing]. With the exception of royal palaces (kraton), monumental mosques and defensive masonry redoubts, urban housing was constructed from perishable timber, bamboo, rattan and thatch, elevated on stilts along riverbanks and tidal estuaries [@Widodo2018Morphology].

These coastal port polities (bandar) exhibited fluid demographic boundaries. Urban populations clustered along navigable waterways, facilitating immediate waterborne transport and rapid evacuation during hostile naval raids [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Kemper2019Umbilical]. Major ports were organised into designated residential quarters (kampung) administered by community headmen (syahbandar) who oversaw foreign merchant communities, including Gujeratis, Tamils, Bengalis, Arabs, Persians, Javanese, Bugis and Chinese [@Subrahmanyam2020Coromandel; @Ownby2016Secret]. In cities such as Melaka, Banten and Makassar, extensive enslaved and bonded populations performed vital functions in domestic labour, artisanal crafts and portage, sustaining the commercial infrastructure of the emporia [@Raben2008Cities; @Knaap2006About]. This polyethnic organisation insulated urban trade from agrarian disruptions, though it rendered port settlements susceptible to catastrophic fires and sudden demographic dispersal [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Raben2008Cities].

## Pre-Spanish Philippine Barangays and Alluvial Thalassocracies

Prior to the arrival of Spanish colonial expeditions under Ferdinand Magellan (1521AD) and Miguel Lopez de Legazpi (1565AD), the Philippine archipelago was characterised by decentralised coastal and riverine polities known as barangays [@M2021Multiple; @Bjork1998Link]. Ranging in size from several dozen to several hundred households (typically numbering between 100 and 2.000 inhabitants), barangays were led by hereditary chiefs (datu) and supported by free warriors (maharlika, timawa) and dependent debtor-servants (alipin, oripun) [@M2021Multiple; @Clav2025Beyond].

In strategically positioned coastal embayments and river confluences, larger confederations and fortified coastal towns emerged:
- Tondo and Maynila: Situated on opposite banks of the Pasig River where it debouches into Manila Bay, these twin polities controlled trade between Chinese junks and the agricultural communities of the Laguna de Bay basin, establishing maritime ties with the Sultanate of Brunei prior to Spanish conquest [@Bjork1998Link; @Morris1974Brunei].
- Butuan and Cebu: In the Visayas and northern Mindanao, coastal settlements engaged in gold extraction, regional boat building and long-distance oceanic navigation, evidenced by large plank-built edge-pegged watercraft (balangay) dating to the mediaeval era [@Green1995Interim].
- Mindanao and Sulu: Interior river basins along the Pulangi River and the island archipelagos of Sulu supported sophisticated polities whose social structures, oral lineages and manuscript traditions documented extensive regional interaction [@Clav2025Beyond; @Mendoza2015Landlessness]. Communal gong-chime ensembles and musical traditions linked these southern polities to broader Austronesian and maritime networks [@Ellorin2026Virtuosos], while insular husbandry of domestic fowl reflected durable maritime exchange across the Sulu Archipelago [@MJB2025Insights].

# Methodology

## Spatial Grid and Dasymetric Covariates

To model demographic distributions across 2.073.299 km² of land area, MANDALA partitions the maritime domain into 26.777 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells. Each cell is evaluated against environmental, topographical and nautical covariates calibrated to pre-colonial settlement patterns [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Jones2018Some]:
- Coastal and estuarine proximity: Exponential distance decay penalising inland cells in rugged island interiors while rewarding coastal margins within 10 km of navigable water [@Widodo2018Morphology].
- Fluvial network buffering: Proximity to major river arteries (the Brantas and Solo in Java, the Musi and Batanghari in Sumatra, the Kapuas and Barito in Borneo, the Pampanga and Pasig in Luzon) essential for inland transport and alluvial agriculture [@Jones2018Some; @Knaap2006About].
- Volcanic soil fertility: Soil classification layers distinguishing nutrient-rich volcanic andosols in Java, Bali and southern Luzon from nutrient-poor podsols and tropical peat swamps in Borneo and eastern Sumatra [@Wood2008Volcano; @Faral2022Year].
- Topographic relief: Slope penalties applied to rugged cordilleras (the Barisan Range of Sumatra, the Central Cordillera of Luzon, the Crocker Range of Borneo) that restricted dense sedentary settlement to highland valleys [@M2021Multiple].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To prevent demographic double counting between nucleated urban settlements and rural agrarian populations, 2.422 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are directly anchored to their WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year (1200AD, 1400AD, 1500AD, 1565AD, 1600AD, 1700AD and 1786AD), the active population of catalogued settlements inside each sub-region is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope [@Singru2015Regional; @Jones2018Some].

The residual rural population is subsequently distributed across non-settled terrestrial pixels in proportion to dasymetric suitability weights. A boundary feathering filter smoothes transition zones across sub-regional borders, preventing artificial density cliffs across straits and mountain watersheds.

## Calibrating Archival and Archaeological Envelopes

Sub-regional benchmark population totals are anchored to comprehensive historiographical and archaeological records [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Raben2008Cities]. For Java, demographic envelopes reconcile epigraphic land grants (sima), VOC taxation registers, rice-yield surveys and military troop enumerations recorded in court chronicles and colonial dispatches [@Wood2008Volcano; @Knaap2006About]. For the Malay Peninsula, Melaka and peninsular sultanate registers provide benchmark checks [@DeJosselinDe1960Malacca; @Borschberg2016Melaka]. For the Philippines, pre-1565AD figures are calibrated against archaeological site surveys, porcelain sherd concentrations and early Spanish tribute censuses (Relacion de las Islas Filipinas by Miguel de Loarca in 1582AD and Antonio de Morga in 1609AD), tracking the subsequent fiscal and demographic reorganisation of the archipelago [@Bjork1998Link; @Clav2025Beyond].

Table \ref{tab:subregions} documents the eight sub-regions, their land areas, benchmark populations from 1200AD to 1786AD and peak terminal densities.

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_1200 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1200"]])
  p_1400 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1400"]])
  p_1500 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1500"]])
  p_1565 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1565"]])
  p_1600 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1600"]])
  p_1700 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1700"]])
  p_1786 <- as.numeric(r$population[["1786"]])
  dens_1786 <- p_1786 / a * 100
  data.frame(
    Region = if (!is.null(reg_short[[rk]])) reg_short[[rk]] else clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P1200AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1200),
    P1400AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1400),
    P1500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1500),
    P1565AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1565),
    P1600AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1600),
    P1700AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1700),
    P1786AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_1786),
    Density1786 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_1786, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P1200AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1200),
  P1400AD = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1400"]])),
  P1500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1500"]])),
  P1565AD = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1565"]])),
  P1600AD = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1600"]])),
  P1700AD = viscount_fmt_pop(as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["1700"]])),
  P1786AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_1786),
  Density1786 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_1786 / tot_area * 100, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark populations and 1786AD terminal density across maritime Southeast Asia.",
  c("Sub-Region", "Area km² (Share)", "1200AD", "1400AD", "1500AD", "1565AD", "1600AD", "1700AD", "1786AD", "1786AD Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Testing and Validation

## Ceramic Sequences and External Trade Ware Assemblages

Archaeological verification of pre-colonial demographic nucleations relies heavily on quantified ceramic assemblages [@SAKAI1993Hizen; @Ownby2016Secret]. Because local domestic pottery was unglazed and prone to rapid weathering in tropical soils, imported Chinese, Vietnamese, Thai and Japanese high-fired glazed ceramics provide robust chronological markers and proxies for commercial density [@SAKAI1993Hizen; @Subrahmanyam2020Coromandel].

Extensive excavations across Manila, Santa Ana, Cebu, Butuan, Kota Cina in northern Sumatra, Banten in western Java and Trowulan in eastern Java demonstrate a marked expansion in ceramic deposition rates between the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries [@SAKAI1993Hizen; @Widodo2018Morphology]. In Banten, stratigraphical analyses confirm the dense circulation of seventeenth-century Japanese Hizen porcelain alongside Chinese wares, illustrating direct maritime exchanges mediated by the Zheng commercial network and regional merchant guilds [@SAKAI1993Hizen]. At Trowulan, the fourteen-square-kilometre urban capital of Majapahit, surface sherd surveys reveal thousands of metric tonnes of Chinese celadon and blue-and-white porcelain, confirming an urban agglomeration approaching 100k inhabitants during the fourteenth century [@Widodo2018Morphology].

## Zooarchaeological and Marine Foraging Constraints

Faunal analysis of stratified deposits across coastal shell middens and riverine settlement mounds validates nutritional carrying capacities [@Green1995Interim; @MJB2025Insights]. Excavations at coastal sites across the Philippines, southern Sulawesi and the Moluccas document a dietary regime heavily reliant on pelagic and inshore marine taxa, including groupers (*Serranidae*), snappers (*Lutjanidae*), jacks (*Carangidae*) and mangrove molluscs (*Anadara*, *Geloina*) [@Green1995Interim; @Faral2022Year].

In inland agrarian centres, zooarchaeological assemblages are dominated by domesticated water buffalo (*Bubalus bubalis*), pigs (*Sus scrofa*) and village fowl (*Gallus gallus*), reflecting intensive draught labour for wetland rice tillage and communal domestic consumption [@Wood2008Volcano; @MJB2025Insights]. In insular settings such as Tidore and Ternate, volcanic soils supported specialised horticultural regimes, including spice orchards and tuber production, which sustained island populations despite periodic volcanic disturbances [@Faral2022Year; @Kadir2025Consumer].

## Architectural Masonry and Settlement Morphology

While vernacular domestic dwellings utilised organic materials, pre-colonial elites invested in monumental brick masonry, stone ramparts and hydraulic works [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Arifia2024Batee]. At Banten Lama, the seventeenth-century sultanate palace and Grand Mosque incorporated sophisticated fired-brick engineering, vaulted doorways and hydraulic canals influenced by regional and European design [@Arifia2024Batee; @Kemper2019Umbilical]. At Melaka, structural and defensive complexes reflected the transition from sultanate royal enclosures to early colonial fortifications [@Mustaffa2023Tracing; @Borschberg2016Melaka]. At Somba Opu, the fortress capital of Gowa in southern Sulawesi, builders erected brick walls up to two metres thick with clay-mortar binding to withstand naval artillery [@Widodo2018Morphology].

Funerary archaeology and historical epidemiological records provide direct mortality profiles and demographic health indicators [@Kraft2013Stagnant; @Arifia2024Batee]. Skeletal series excavated from pre-Spanish Philippine burial sites at Maitum (Sarangani) and churchyards at Santa Cruz and Cebu reveal infant mortality rates typical of early modern pre-transitional regimes (approximately 25% to 35% infant mortality before age five), accompanied by low incidence of chronic infectious skeletal lesions, indicating adequate caloric nutrition in coastal agrarian zones [@Kraft2013Stagnant; @M2021Multiple].

## Four-Wave Saturation Audit

The MANDALA settlement database was compiled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion process to ensure complete regional coverage:
- Wave 1: Automated extraction of official national registries and historical gazetteers, establishing a baseline of 1.502 catalogued settlements.
- Wave 2: Archival monographs, excavation catalogues and regional colonial administrative reports, contributing 654 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits, adding 266 mediaeval and early modern trading localities.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap hunting and homonym audits, confirming zero unaccounted settlements (marginal gain 0,0%).

In total, 2.549 candidate settlements were audited: 2.422 were accepted and 127 were excluded (primarily duplicate survey aliases within 2,2 km or non-habitation anchorages).

# Results

## Demographic Trajectory and Benchmark Analysis

The demographic trajectory of maritime Southeast Asia from 1200AD to 1786AD demonstrates sustained growth punctuated by regional political realignments and external trade reorganisations (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r fig-trajectory, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_pre_colonial_sultanates_and_philippines_demography.png",
  "Demographic trajectory of maritime Southeast Asia and the Philippines (1200AD to 1786AD), illustrating benchmark population expansion across eight insular sub-regions, the rise of trading sultanates and eighteenth-century agrarian growth.",
  "fig:trajectory"
)
```

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("1200", "1400", "1500", "1565", "1600", "1700", "1786")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  p_jav <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_java_sultanates$population[[yk]])
  p_sum <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_aceh_sumatra$population[[yk]])
  p_luz <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_prehispanic_luzon_visayas$population[[yk]])
  p_pen <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_malacca_peninsula$population[[yk]])
  p_sul <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_makassar_sulawesi$population[[yk]])
  p_bor <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_brunei_borneo$population[[yk]])
  p_sulu <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_sulu_mindanao$population[[yk]])
  p_mal <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$pcs_ternate_tidore_maluku$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area * 100
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = fmt_yr(yk),
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    Java = viscount_fmt_pop(p_jav),
    Sumatra = viscount_fmt_pop(p_sum),
    LuzonVis = viscount_fmt_pop(p_luz),
    Peninsula = viscount_fmt_pop(p_pen),
    Sulawesi = viscount_fmt_pop(p_sul),
    Borneo = viscount_fmt_pop(p_bor),
    SuluMind = viscount_fmt_pop(p_sulu),
    Maluku = viscount_fmt_pop(p_mal),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and sub-regional distribution across maritime Southeast Asia (1200AD to 1786AD).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density", "Java", "Sumatra", "Luzon-Vis", "Peninsula", "Sulawesi", "Borneo", "Sulu-Mind", "Maluku"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Four Historical Demographic Epochs

### High Mediaeval Maritime Expansion (1200AD to 1400AD)

Between 1200AD and 1400AD, maritime Southeast Asia grew from 7,50M to 9,40M inhabitants (an aggregate expansion of 25,3%, with regional density rising from 361,74 to 453,38 persons per 100 km²). This period coincided with the climax of the Majapahit empire in eastern Java, whose tributary mandala connected riverine ports across Java, Bali, Madura, southern Sumatra and coastal Borneo [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Jones2018Some].

Trowulan operated as the royal capital, concentrating royal courts, craft workshops, markets and foreign merchant enclaves across an area exceeding 100 km² [@Widodo2018Morphology]. Java accounted for 3,15M people in 1200AD, rising to 3,95M in 1400AD. Across northern Sumatra, Samudera Pasai emerged as an Islamic maritime gateway, while Temasek flourished as a riverine trading settlement commanding the Singapore Strait before its devastation around 1398AD [@DeJosselinDe1960Malacca; @Borschberg2016Melaka]. In the Philippines, regional trading polities expanded at Tondo, Cebu and Butuan, exchanging forest and marine products for Chinese Song and Yuan ceramics [@Green1995Interim; @M2021Multiple].

### Age of Commerce and Sultanate Apex (1400AD to 1565AD)

The fifteenth and sixteenth centuries constituted the classic Age of Commerce in maritime Southeast Asia, with regional population increasing from 9,40M in 1400AD to 10,80M in 1500AD and 11,60M by 1565AD. The founding and meteoric rise of the Sultanate of Melaka transformed global trade geography [@DeJosselinDe1960Malacca; @Borschberg2016Melaka; @Subrahmanyam2020Coromandel]. Melaka grew into an emporium of nearly 100k residents, accommodating merchant fleets from across Afro-Eurasia and codifying institutional customs that governed regional commerce [@Tachimoto1998Malacca; @Zaharani2025Concept].

Following the Portuguese conquest of Melaka in 1511AD, regional trade restructured rather than collapsed:
- Trade dispersed toward rival Islamic sultanates: Aceh expanded its naval and commercial reach in Sumatra, while Banten captured the pepper trade of western Java and southern Sumatra [@Arifia2024Batee; @Kemper2019Umbilical].
- The Sultanate of Demak led an Islamic maritime alliance on the north coast of Java that dismantled Majapahit hegemony and founded Jayakarta (modern Jakarta) in 1527AD after expelling Portuguese forces from the port of Sunda Kelapa [@Widodo2018Morphology].
- In the eastern seas, Ternate and Tidore competed for dominance over the clove trade of Maluku, while Brunei established an expansive maritime sultanate controlling the coasts of northern Borneo, Sulu and the western Visayas [@Morris1974Brunei; @Harrison1973Brunei; @Rusdiyanto2018Kesultanan].
- In Luzon, Tondo and Maynila operated as fortified Muslim-led river polities allied through marriage with the royal house of Brunei, controlling commerce throughout the central Philippine archipelago [@Bjork1998Link; @Morris1974Brunei].

### European Encroachment and Regional Adaptation (1565AD to 1700AD)

Between 1565AD and 1700AD, population expanded from 11,60M to 13,80M, despite direct European military intervention and commercial monopolisation policies. Spanish colonisation of the Philippines commenced with the establishment of Cebu (1565AD) and the conquest of Maynila (1571AD), which was transformed into the walled city of Intramuros and connected to the trans-Pacific Manila Galleon trade with Acapulco [@Bjork1998Link].

Concurrently, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) pursued aggressive armed monopolies in the spice archipelago:
- Banda was depopulated and reorganised into Dutch nutmeg plantations in 1621AD [@Charney1996World].
- Ternate and Tidore were subjected to forced clove tree eradication policies (hongi tochten) to maintain European price controls [@Charney1996World; @Rusdiyanto2018Kesultanan].
- In Java, the VOC seized Jayakarta in 1619AD, renaming it Batavia and erecting a stone fortress and European-style canal grid [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Raben2008Cities].
- Simultaneously, the agrarian Sultanate of Mataram unified the interior plains of Central and East Java under Sultan Agung (reigned 1613AD to 1645AD), mounting massive sieges against Dutch Batavia in 1628AD and 1629AD that demonstrated the formidable demographic mobilization capacity of interior Javanese wet-rice agriculture [@Wood2008Volcano; @Knaap2006About].
- In southern Sulawesi, the Sultanate of Gowa-Tallo defended its policy of free trade from its fortress city of Somba Opu until its defeat by a combined Dutch and Bugis force under Arung Palakka in the Makassar War (1666AD to 1669AD) [@Raben2008Cities; @Knaap2006About].
- In western Java, the Sultanate of Banten resisted Dutch encirclement by diversifying diplomatic and merchant alliances with English, Danish, French and Chinese trading factions until VOC intervention in 1682AD [@Kemper2019Umbilical; @SAKAI1993Hizen].

### Eighteenth-Century Agrarian Consolidation (1700AD to 1786AD)

The eighteenth century witnessed substantial agrarian consolidation and population growth across the archipelago, expanding from 13,80M in 1700AD to 15,80M by 1786AD. Java remained the primary engine of demographic expansion, growing from 5,80M to 6,64M inhabitants (an aggregate density of 4.947,92 persons per 100 km²).

Following the Treaty of Giyanti in 1755AD, the Mataram sultanate was partitioned into the rival courts of Surakarta (Kartasura) and Yogyakarta (Kotagede and Plered), initiating a period of relative peace in the interior that stimulated wet-rice expansion, village foundation and rural market formation [@Wood2008Volcano; @Knaap2006About]. In the Philippines, the colonial administration implemented the reduccion policy, concentrating dispersed rural barangays into compact pueblos centred on Spanish stone churches, plazas and administrative buildings [@Bjork1998Link; @Singru2015Regional]. Concurrently, the Sultanate of Sulu attained its peak commercial expansion, conducting maritime raiding and trade across the Sulu and Celebes seas to feed the British tea and opium trade in Canton [@Clav2025Beyond; @Mendoza2015Landlessness; @Ellorin2026Virtuosos]. In the spice islands, formal sultanate traditions and regalia maintained indigenous authority alongside Dutch commercial footholds [@Clercq1890Staatsievl; @Rusdiyanto2018Kesultanan].

## Urban Hierarchy and Leading Centres

Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} documents the leading fifteen catalogued settlements across maritime Southeast Asia ordered by peak historical population.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_1600 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["1600"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["1600"]]) else "-"
  p_1786 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["1786"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["1786"]]) else "-"
  coord_str <- fmt_coord(s$coords)
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(reg_short[[s$region_id]])) reg_short[[s$region_id]] else clean_text(s$region)
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P1600AD = if (is.numeric(p_1600)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_1600) else "-",
    P1786AD = if (is.numeric(p_1786)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_1786) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading fifteen pre-colonial and early modern settlements in maritime Southeast Asia, showing coordinates, peak population and benchmark populations.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Sub-Region", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "1600AD Pop", "1786AD Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Structural Hierarchy of Pre-Colonial Settlements

Settlements across the archipelago exhibited a clear functional hierarchy:
1. Primary agrarian capitals and colonial metropolises (> 100k inhabitants):
   - Setiabudi and the Greater Batavia urban complex in western Java, expanding rapidly from 149,43k in 1600AD to 313,99k in 1786AD through immigration of Chinese merchants, Bugis sailors and Javanese labourers [@Raben2008Cities; @Knaap2006About].
   - Tondo on Manila Bay, accommodating 149,02k inhabitants at its peak in 1500AD as the preeminent pre-colonial riverine emporium of Luzon [@Bjork1998Link; @M2021Multiple].
   - Jayakarta (135,32k peak in 1700AD) and Surabaya (128,22k peak in 1600AD), anchoring maritime trade and naval power along the northern coast of Java [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Knaap2006About].
   - The royal Mataram capitals of Kotagede and Plered (116,22k peak in 1700AD) and Kartasura (101,83k peak in 1700AD), concentrating administrative nobility, palace guards and agrarian tribute in the fertile volcanic plains of Central Java [@Wood2008Volcano].
2. Major regional entrepôts and provincial centres (50k to 100k inhabitants):
   - Melaka, the premier trade hub of the fifteenth century (98,63k peak in 1600AD), maintaining commercial centrality following its Portuguese capture [@Borschberg2016Melaka; @Mustaffa2023Tracing].
   - Trowulan (97,75k peak in 1400AD), the expansive urban capital of the Majapahit empire [@Widodo2018Morphology].
   - Banten Lama (90,10k peak in 1700AD), the pepper-exporting capital of western Java [@Kemper2019Umbilical; @SAKAI1993Hizen].
   - Makassar and Somba Opu (89,09k peak in 1600AD), coordinating the free-trade spice trade of eastern Indonesia [@Raben2008Cities; @Knaap2006About].
   - Banda Aceh (81,70k peak in 1600AD), the naval bastion and Islamic intellectual capital of northern Sumatra [@Arifia2024Batee].
   - Temasek (77,17k peak in 1565AD), anchoring trade at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula [@DeJosselinDe1960Malacca].
3. Secondary riverine and coastal trading ports (20k to 50k inhabitants):
   - Banjarmasin in southern Borneo (36,04k peak in 1786AD), directing pepper and diamond trade along the Barito River.
   - Ternate (24,20k peak in 1786AD) and Tidore in Maluku, commanding the global clove monopoly [@Rusdiyanto2018Kesultanan; @Charney1996World; @Faral2022Year].
   - Jolo in the Sulu Archipelago (24,01k peak in 1786AD), serving as the fortified island capital of the Sultanate of Sulu [@Clav2025Beyond; @Mendoza2015Landlessness].
   - Brunei Kota Batu, anchoring trade across northern Borneo and the western Visayas [@Morris1974Brunei; @Harrison1973Brunei].
4. Tertiary rural barangays and swidden hamlets (< 20k inhabitants):
   - Thousands of riverine and coastal villages catalogued across the archipelago, sustaining local fishing, subsistence rice cultivation and forest extraction [@Singru2015Regional; @M2021Multiple].

# Limitations

Historical demographic analysis in maritime Southeast Asia faces several methodological constraints:
1. Perishable vernacular architecture: The reliance on timber, bamboo and thatch rather than monumental stone or kiln-fired brick means that residential footprints are rarely preserved in tropical soils, necessitating reliance on ceramic scatter density and historical chronicles [@Widodo2018Morphology; @Jones2018Some].
2. Tropical soil acidity and taphonomic degradation: High humidity, seasonal monsoon rains and acidic tropical soils accelerate the degradation of organic matter and unglazed pottery, limiting stratigraphical bone preservation in lowland sites [@Green1995Interim; @Faral2022Year].
3. Fluid settlement mobility: Coastal and riverine communities frequently relocated settlements following hostile naval raids, epidemic outbreaks or river channel shifts, complicating longitudinal site boundary delineation [@Raben2008Cities; @Clav2025Beyond].
4. Heterogeneous colonial documentation: Early Spanish tribute records in the Philippines and VOC registers in Java utilised differing accounting units (tributos, cabezas, family hearths), requiring careful conversion multipliers to maintain comparative consistency across sub-regions [@Bjork1998Link; @Jones2018Some].

# Conclusion

The pre-colonial sultanates of the Malay Archipelago and the pre-Spanish Philippines supported a resilient and expansive demographic system that grew from 7,50M inhabitants in 1200AD to 15,80M by 1786AD across 2,07M km² of insular and coastal territory. Driven by the complementary dynamics of intensive sawah rice agriculture in the volcanic heartlands of Java and Sumatra, swidden cultivation and coastal foraging in the outer islands, and high-value entrepôt trade linking the Indian Ocean with East Asia, the region fostered sophisticated forms of waterborne urbanism.

The arrival of European mercantile powers in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries fundamentally altered international trade routes and suppressed independent indigenous sultanates, yet it did not halt regional demographic expansion. Instead, populations reorganised across resilient interior agricultural basins and alternative maritime circuits, laying the demographic foundations for modern Southeast Asian states.

# Appendix

The MANDALA source ledger audited 2.549 candidate settlement records, resulting in 2.422 accepted localities and 127 documented exclusions. Table \ref{tab:saturation} presents the four-wave asymptotic saturation audit demonstrating complete regional coverage.

```{r tbl-saturation, results='asis'}
sat_waves <- led_data$saturation_audit$waves
sat_rows <- lapply(sat_waves, function (w) {
  data.frame(
    Wave = paste0("Wave ", w$wave),
    SourceClass = clean_text(w$source_class),
    PriorTotal = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$prior_cumulative_included), 0L),
    NewlyIncluded = viscount_fmt_number(as.numeric(w$newly_included), 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sat <- do.call(rbind, sat_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_sat,
  "Four-wave asymptotic saturation audit of catalogued settlements across maritime Southeast Asia.",
  c("Ingestion Wave", "Source Category", "Prior Cumulative", "Newly Included"),
  list(label = "tab:saturation", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```
